description: Voting Village talks from DEF CON 34. These recordings are on the DEF CON media server, not YouTube.

talks.title: Internet Voting - Trust Us, It's Secure
talks.teaser: Makes the case that internet voting cannot be secured or verified, using past pilot breaches, failed trials and expert reviews as evidence.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the speaker's own change of view: a 1999 National Science Foundation workshop convinced her that returning voted ballots over the internet could not be made safe. She defines internet voting as sending a completed ballot electronically, by web, email or fax, and notes that 33 states plus the District of Columbia allow some form of it, mostly for overseas and military voters. Her core objection is that the secret ballot leaves voters no way to confirm that a ballot arrived and was counted correctly.

The middle of the talk is a run of case studies. A 2004 review of the SERVE overseas system led to its cancellation. A 2010 District of Columbia test was broken by university researchers who changed cast ballots and reached into the surrounding network. Australia's iVote system drew repeated flaw reports, and the Voatz mobile app was shown to let attackers alter votes. Canadian and Swiss studies found no turnout gain from online voting, and Estonia's long-running system was questioned in later analyses. Vendors often answered critics by disputing findings or pushing to discredit them.

She closes with a practical list: hand-marked paper ballots, strong chain of custody, risk-limiting audits, honest officials, and no internet return of ballots. For overseas and disabled voters, she urges officials to promote blank-ballot downloads and remote accessible vote-by-mail instead.

talks.title: On the Weaponization of Voting Channels
talks.teaser: Argues that differences between voting channels, such as internet and mail-in ballots, can be weaponized to erode public trust in election results.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a computer scientist who has observed elections as an international delegate, starts from a worry: when a country offers several ways to vote, the results from each channel can differ, and those gaps can be exploited to undermine confidence in an outcome. He points to a 2020 Pennsylvania results screen whose lead appeared to shift as mail-in ballots were counted, and argues that public trust matters as much as accurate counting.

The main case study is Estonia, which lets voters cast ballots online or on paper. In the 2023 count, preliminary results appeared stable after the internet votes were checked against paper records, then changed sharply when internet ballots were uploaded. A party that had told supporters to avoid internet voting lost about half of its apparent support and challenged the result in the Supreme Court, which dismissed the case on procedural grounds. A survey with a political scientist colleague found a significant drop in trust in internet voting, with the political extremes losing confidence most.

He closes with untested ideas: withholding channel-level breakdowns, publishing no preliminary results, moving to a single uniform channel, and creating independent bodies that run channel-specific risk-limiting audits. He admits these are rough and may not be practical. The takeaway for practitioners is that trust in each voting channel needs protecting, and election officials should plan for it before it is exploited.

talks.title: Election Observation - Merely Allowing People to Watch is Not Enough
talks.teaser: Argues that election observation needs designed programs, legal access, shared documentation and technical expertise, not just admitting people to watch.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by asking why election observation is needed at all. The speaker argues that voters cannot simply trust election administrators, since history shows that most election misconduct comes from officials and that ordinary carelessness is common, especially across the roughly two million people who run a US election. He calls for a modest, institutionalized distrust that keeps people paying attention.

The middle of the talk catalogs barriers. Some states limit each party to one observer per polling place, which shuts out insurgent candidates. Photographing voted ballots is banned in ways that also block useful documentation. Vendors often bind counties with NDAs over procedure manuals, and a Dutch internet voting case showed key generation happening behind closed doors. Observers also face hard problems: a helpline that could issue replacement credentials, a control that is impossible to prove absent, a test that failed a sanity check, and seal logs and zero tapes that were ritualized rather than checked. Long shifts and frayed staff make access harder still.

The speaker concludes that effective observation requires organization. Partisan, nonpartisan and international missions each have roles, with passive observers producing reports and active observers intervening quickly. Teams need legal and technical members, and they need to share data. He argues for open training materials, a public record of observations and observer access to the same documentation election staff use. The takeaway for practitioners is that admitting people to the room is not enough without a design that makes the process verifiable.

talks.title: Low Skill, High Impact Attacks that Could Derail Internet Voting
talks.teaser: Shows how cheap, low-skill attacks such as website defacement, malicious voting apps, and phone-based misdirection could erode voter confidence in internet voting.
talks.summary:
Local election administrator John Odum argues that large-scale internet voting will never earn the public trust needed for a credible election. He points to a 2024 survey in which only 36% of respondents had confidence in votes cast over the internet, and he contends that attacks aimed at confidence deserve as much attention as attacks that alter ballots.

He then walks through inexpensive options a moderately skilled adversary could use. These include defacing county election websites, publishing voter-history data to create false claims, phishing for content management system credentials, and distributing malicious voting apps or browser extensions. He also covers low-cost denial-of-service stressors that can take down a single county site and generate headlines. The most concerning case, in his view, is vote by phone. Using New Hampshire as an example, he estimates how many voters could be misdirected from purchased mobile contact lists, and he notes that a race decided by a tiny margin could be swung without changing any votes.

He closes by saying decentralization, usually seen as the strength of the American system, becomes an exposure when every jurisdiction runs its own online channel. The Q&A covered legislator education, the risk of a slippery slope toward wider online voting, and postage for absentee voters as an alternative. He presented the talk as a warning rather than a how-to, and offered no clear fix.

talks.title: The Republic is a Team Sport
talks.teaser: Hosts a facilitated closing discussion on election trust, transparency, and misinformation, ending with what attendees can do next.
talks.summary:
Kendall Spencer closes the Voting Village week without slides, opening a facilitated discussion meant to move attendees from listening to deciding what comes next for democracy. The room starts with what people heard during the week, and the talk quickly turns to how algorithm-driven short video clips shape what citizens see, leaving little time for slower reading and reflection.

The conversation then moves to what is broken. Participants debate whether election transparency can rebuild public confidence, and whether voter identification is needed, with one side citing past studies that found few documented fraud cases and the other arguing that access to ID must come before any requirement. Several people observe that different audiences now receive different information feeds, so they cannot agree on the facts underneath their disagreements. Spencer repeatedly returns to education and people's ability to reason through what they read.

Spencer closes by framing the core problem as a lack of time and habits for questioning information, and argues that every person has a role in challenging ideas constructively. His practical takeaways are to share verified facts within personal networks, which people tend to trust more than algorithmic feeds, and to pair transparency with accessible, consistent rules for voters.

talks.title: Pulling Back the Curtain on the Voting Booth
talks.teaser: Shows how a known Dominion voting machine flaw, a predictable record-ID sequence, let an AI agent link Georgia ballots back to individual voters.
talks.summary:
The talk revisits a 2022 flaw in Dominion voting systems. Scanners tag each ballot with a number meant to be random for shuffling the records, but the numbers come from a fixed arithmetic sequence. Because the sequence is predictable, anyone with the public cast vote records can reverse it, recover the order in which ballots were scanned, and tie ballots to voters. The flaw does not change tallies, but it breaks the promise that nobody can tell how a person voted.

The speakers describe how a Georgia advocate with no coding background used a chatbot to reproduce the recovery from public Georgia files and the research paper. The agent reportedly grouped voters into buckets by check-in time, party and ballot type, and claimed it could attribute roughly 1.5 million in-person ballots. The speakers stress that these are the model's own claims, that models make mistakes, and that the work took about an hour or two on a commute, which they argue shows that exploits once requiring specialist weeks are now quick to run.

The session closes with the policy fight in Georgia. The Secretary of State declined to apply the available vendor patch and ordered counties to stop releasing records with record IDs, a step the speakers say does not stop insiders and vendors from accessing them. They ask for the patch, redacted records, sanitizing tools for old data, and no new records containing reversible numbers. Their broader point is that obfuscation is not a substitute for real randomness or encryption, and that AI lowers the barrier to exploiting known weaknesses.

talks.title: Liberty and Justice for All
talks.teaser: Presents a state election CISO's view of threats to election offices, covering a website attack, the recent primary, and physical, reputational and logistical risks.
talks.summary:
The talk is given by the chief information security officer for Arizona's Secretary of State office, who explains why election officials are often reluctant to speak openly about attacks. He recounts a June 2025 defacement of the state's candidate results site, which he assesses with high confidence was carried out by Iranian actors. The office detected and recovered quickly with help from state homeland security, the National Guard and partners, then shared indicators of compromise without attribution. That openness was later used against leadership in political fights, which he presents as a reason sharing could decline.

The middle section walks through the recent Arizona primary, moved to July 21 to leave time for recounts. Monsoon storms caused power outages, intermittent internet and road closures, and several counties reported ballot delivery problems. He describes a fusion-center setup on election days, a state program that supplies security controls free to small counties, and guidance on using AI tools carefully in under-resourced offices. His threat survey covers bomb threats, white powder mailings, drone electioneering, active shooter risk, swatting, phishing and vishing, payroll and finance fraud, insider risk, and LLM and search poisoning.

He closes with advice for the general election: expect honest mistakes and separate them from malice, demand evidence, report problems to officials instead of only the media, and take part in the process through observing, poll work and early voting.

talks.title: Are We Making Things Worse Election Denialism and Security Research
talks.teaser: Election security panelists examine how vulnerability research gets misread as proof of stolen votes, and how experts can communicate findings without eroding public trust.
talks.summary:
This Voting Village panel, moderated by a DEF CON board attorney, brings together Michael Moore, Arizona's Secretary of State chief information security officer, statistics professor Philip Stark, and Jeff Hail of the Center for Democracy and Technology, a former CISA election security official. The opening question asks how a vulnerability differs from proof that an election outcome was wrong. The panelists agree the two are distinct: a weakness existing does not mean anyone exploited it. They argue the larger problem is communication, because the public often hears a vulnerability as incompetence or as evidence of theft, and partisan framing makes that worse.

The discussion then moves to trust and relationships. Stark described auditing a 2021 New Hampshire election that drew hostile reaction and threats, and said a reporter's advice helped him explain technical problems in ways that did not inflame people. Several speakers warned that technical complexity is often used as a stand-in for authority, and that security experts should step in when claims misrepresent their data. The conversation also covered audits: a paper trail that cannot be trusted makes any audit or recount meaningless, and post-election audits often happen under time pressure before certification.

The closing message is that imperfections should be acknowledged rather than hidden, but never overclaimed. Panelists urged practitioners to speak with legislators, to focus spending on risks that have been measured, and to build agreement on a few shared facts before debating remedies. For anyone working on elections or on disclosure, the takeaway is that accurate, plain-language explanation is part of the security work.

talks.title: Welcome to Voting Village 2026
talks.teaser: Introduces the DEF CON Voting Village's origins, its founders, and the election security research planned for the 2026 program.
talks.summary:
This opening session kicks off the 2026 Voting Village at DEF CON 34, the tenth year the Election Integrity Foundation has run it. Founders and board members introduce themselves and explain why they care about election security. The origin story is recounted: after a 2016 Library of Congress exemption to the DMCA covered good-faith research on voting equipment, a group bought voting machines on eBay. That protected them from manufacturer threats, and the open community began examining the hardware.

The speakers describe how the village grew from a room of machines into a venue for technical election security research. The first year surfaced vulnerabilities that earlier academic studies had missed. Preview highlights for the weekend include a first public account of an analysis of Puerto Rico voting equipment that the federal government seized and never published, and a talk on ballot deanonymization in Georgia. A hacking lab with equipment and background write-ups sits next door, and election officials attend to learn and share problems.

The speakers note that vendors remain wary of the village, and that the adversarial relationship from earlier years has not fully gone away. Their takeaway is that open examination and disclosure are how weaknesses get fixed, and that informed debate depends on tested facts rather than denial. Recordings are promised on YouTube after some post-processing.

talks.title: RLA Workshop
talks.teaser: Walks attendees through a hands-on risk-limiting audit of a mock mayoral election, showing how random ballot sampling can confirm a reported winner.
talks.summary:
The workshop runs a live demonstration of a risk-limiting audit using a mock mayoral election at the Voting Village. The presenter sets up the premise: a reported result says one candidate beat the others, and an auditor must check, with stated confidence, that the reported winner really won. The paper ballots carry serial numbers, so a specific ballot can be pulled from its precinct and read.

To choose ballots at random, the audience rolls two ten-sided dice to produce a number from zero to 99, which maps to a ballot. Each ballot is compared against a running tally for each winner-loser pair. A ballot for the reported winner nudges the tally up by one, while a ballot for the loser pushes it down by a larger amount, so the tally only climbs toward the stopping point when the sample consistently supports the outcome. The group works through both pairs until each reaches its threshold, which took thirteen ballots in this run. A parallel column shows how the same draws would look if the reported winner were wrong, drifting away from the stop point.

The takeaway is that a small random sample can confirm a wide-margin outcome with high confidence, and the tally rule is simple enough to run by hand. The presenter notes that sampling with replacement keeps the arithmetic easy, while the without-replacement version requires values that change with each draw and is better left to software.

talks.title: What Election Security Researchers Need to Know about DMCA Section 1201
talks.teaser: Explains how DMCA Section 1201 affects election security researchers, covering technical protection measures, the narrow statutory exemptions, and the temporary good-faith research exemption.
talks.summary:
Tori Noble, a staff attorney at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, opens by describing Section 1201 of the DMCA as a 1990s anti-piracy law that became a major legal obstacle for security research, including work on election systems. She separates its two prongs, the anti-circumvention rule and the anti-trafficking rule, and explains what counts as a technical protection measure. She notes that courts have said little on the boundaries, and that treating something as outside the law is risky without counsel.

She then walks through the two statutory exemptions, security testing and encryption research, and explains why both are narrow. The main relief comes from a temporary administrative exemption that security researchers, including Voting Village leaders, won from the Library of Congress. It covers good-faith research on lawfully acquired devices without device-owner permission, but it does not cover trafficking, does not shield against CFAA or copyright claims, must be renewed every three years, and requires that access be solely for research. The lawfully acquired requirement is the main ambiguity, since voting machine companies have argued that resale restrictions in their contracts defeat it.

In the audience questions she addressed fair use, possible constitutional challenges, pre-enforcement suits, and whether donated machines count as lawfully acquired. Her practical advice is to seek written permission from device owners where possible and to follow responsible research practices. She stressed that the talk is general information, not legal advice.

talks.title: We Pwn Your Phone, We Pwn Your Vote (Demo and Panel)
talks.teaser: Demonstrates a zero-click iOS exploit chain built from 39 patched flaws, and argues that platform compromise undermines internet voting.
talks.summary:
This closing-day Voting Village session paired a live demonstration with a panel on internet voting. The argument: voting software is only one layer of the attack surface, and the mobile operating system beneath it is equally exposed to state-level attackers. The presenter ran a chain built from 39 patched iOS vulnerabilities against an older device. It moved from a compromised web page through several sandbox escapes, one bypassing pointer authentication, to root access. It then gathered keychain items, cloud tokens, Wi-Fi passwords and messaging databases and sent them to a command server. A race condition slowed the run, so the full collection was not finished on stage.

The panel argued that a flawless voting app cannot be trusted on a compromised phone, since the platform can alter what voters see and record what they do. Code voting would not reliably prevent this, and a platform attacker could block access to a voting site. Speakers also noted that end-to-end verifiable schemes still rely on trusted components, and that dispute resolution after a detected problem is poorly defined. Many states already allow emailed or faxed ballots for overseas voters, which face similar risks.

The takeaway is that voting security is a systems problem spanning device, network and servers. Anyone assessing remote or mobile voting should model the platform as part of the threat, and be skeptical of claims that device security is solved.

talks.title: Dissecting the ICX Frog
talks.teaser: Examines the Android app and configuration complexity of the Dominion ImageCast X voting machine from a software engineering and architecture perspective.
talks.summary:
This talk steps back from individual vulnerabilities to look at how the ImageCast X voting system is engineered. The speakers work on a classic ICX unit that was bought on eBay and is not encumbered by an NDA or protective order, so it can be discussed openly. The classic model runs Android 4.4.4 while the Prime variant runs Android 5.1.1, and the vendor OS appears to be a modified build of the Android Open Source Project.

Using the APK exported from the device, the team decompiled the app to smali and estimated a codebase of roughly 200,000 lines of Java. They found separate code paths for the two hardware types, such as EEPROM-backed counters on one and disk storage on the other. The app shells out to bash for some functions, such as audio alerts, and one tune appears to be a hidden easter egg. The election definition is a zip of about 1,400 files that includes a SQLite database with 22 tables, and one record holds a hex-encoded JSON blob.

The speaker argues that the many configurations and modes, including ballot-marking, DRE with VVPAT, remote-use and full-face ballot modes, create maintenance and deployment problems beyond security. They ask whether single-purpose devices would be a better design. The practical takeaway is that a system's architecture and configuration sprawl deserve scrutiny alongside its certification.

talks.title: Alerts & Warnings in 2026 Elections
talks.teaser: Explains how the reduced federal role in election security is changing threat sharing, and how volunteer and private groups are filling the gap.
talks.summary:
The panel opens with the 2020 election, when foreign actors sent threatening emails to voters in several states, posing as a far-right group. The same campaign included a video showing a stolen voter file, a weakly exposed voter lookup application in Alaska, and a spike in downloads of a military absentee ballot form. Each signal looked small on its own. Federal agencies combined them, attributed the activity within about a day, and briefed election officials and the public quickly. The speakers present that pipeline as a success that depended on trusted relationships between federal agencies and local election offices.

Since then, the panelists say, that federal capacity has shrunk. Jurisdictions that once relied on free federal assessments and scans have built their own testing, response plans, and vendor contracts, but they can no longer learn from incidents happening elsewhere. A volunteer coalition formed in 2025 now issues alerts, guidance, and referrals. Voting system vendors have kept a coordinating council running, and election groups are trying to route vulnerability reports to the right local offices.

In audience questions, the panelists addressed audits and certification, pointing to reconciliation, hand counts, and public certification steps. Their advice to researchers is to build local relationships with election offices before disclosing findings, and to join as poll workers or auditors to see the process firsthand.

talks.title: From Ballots to Code Independently Watching Norway's Election
talks.teaser: Shows how a lone citizen observer used public records requests and scraped election protocols to probe the paper-ballot process in Norway.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a Norwegian observer who was escorted out of a public hand count by police after photographing it. That episode frames the rest of the talk, which asks how paper-ballot elections can still be watched, questioned and checked. The speaker gives a short primer: votes are counted by hand at each polling station, then transported and scanned for a second count that feeds a closed-source national system.

The middle section covers four findings. Ballot stamps bought abroad looked nearly identical to genuine ones, and records requests showed many municipalities using stamps that are easy to copy. A transport box was shown being stuffed in seconds, and an unsealed ballot box was reported on election night. The central system's source code was requested under open records law, but only partial files came back, with later versions withheld on national security grounds. Roughly 739 information requests produced more than a thousand protocol PDFs, which were converted to structured data. The analysis flagged seat changes between counts, large gaps between first and second counts, and ballot-stuffing indicators, many of which traced back to a display bug in an emergency release.

The closing advice is practical. Request in writing that count notes be preserved before election day, since many were discarded. Record who said and ordered what, file complaints quickly because the window is only four days, and observe openly while staying calm. The speaker argues that public scrutiny of election procedures and the software behind them remains rare and is still needed.

talks.title: There and Back Again
talks.teaser: Presents a forensic examination of a Dominion voting system used in a live Puerto Rico election, covering its control, cryptography and software failures.
talks.summary:
The talk recounts how a small forensics team came to examine a Dominion voting system from Puerto Rico after a federal request. They imaged the election management system and several machines, then worked in a conservative threat model: a skilled attacker with access to the local network, not an insider or stolen keys. Much of the effort went into decrypting and deobfuscating self-modifying binaries, and the team had to set aside earlier material with broken chain of custody.

The findings cover four areas. LTE modems were active during operation, so the system was not air-gapped. Passwords were reused, weak or hard-coded, and audit databases shared the attack surface of the main system. Cryptography showed weak entropy, IV reuse, hard-coded material and cleartext key handling. At least twelve high or critical CVEs affected commercial components, with patches available before certification, and the code relied on obfuscation and stored credentials in plain text. The speakers say they found no evidence that votes were altered, but they also could not rule out exploitation with the data they had.

The recommendations push for a constrained, immutable and air-gapped appliance, open source code with reproducible builds and published hashes, and append-only audit logs. They argue that certification should test deployed configurations and real cryptographic use, not only FIPS-validated modules, and that independent risk-limiting audits against paper records are needed. The talk closes by announcing a nonprofit effort to fund open review of voting software.

talks.title: Publicly Auditable Elections
talks.teaser: Explains how publicly auditable, end-to-end verifiable elections let anyone check vote tallies without trusting election software, hardware, or officials.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that hardening election systems is necessary but cannot be enough, so detection through auditing must also be part of the plan. The speaker separates two audit types. Administrative audits, such as risk-limiting audits, are run by officials against physical paper ballots. Public audits can be run by anyone, at any time tallies are released, and check results against the votes voters actually cast, so they need no paper. The speaker claims a public audit can catch any alteration of tallies, including attacks not yet invented.

The mechanism is end-to-end verifiability. Each vote is published as a cryptographic commitment that is bound to the choice but reveals nothing about it. Voters receive a confirmation code they can check on a website or ignore, and anyone can verify that the published commitments add up to the announced totals. Tallying works by multiplying encrypted ballots together, so only addition is needed, followed by a proof of correct decryption. A card trick illustrates how a voter can gain confidence in a hidden vote without being able to prove it to anyone else. The talk also mentions deployed systems and a newer commitment-based variant that needs no keys.

The takeaway is that only a small fraction of voters need to check their receipts for high statistical confidence, and each voter chooses whom to trust. The speaker says internet voting is not yet ready, even with these techniques.

talks.title: The Paper Chase
talks.teaser: Traces how a 2003 California investigation and a failed 2004 primary pushed the state to require paper records and source code review for voting machines.
talks.summary:
The keynote opens with the push toward touchscreen voting after the 2000 Florida recount and the Help America Vote Act. Stanford computer scientist David Dill warned that direct-recording electronic machines left no independent record of each ballot, so errors or manipulation could never be detected. Former California Secretary of State Kevin Shelley describes how he first resisted that argument, then formed a task force in which only three of eleven members backed a voter-verified paper trail.

The middle covers the fallout. Bev Harris found Diebold source code and release notes on a public server, and a state audit showed 17 counties running software that had never been certified. Shelley ordered source disclosure, paper ballots and parallel monitoring, then descertified the TSX in four counties. Machines failed in Alameda and San Diego during the March 2004 primary, and a San Diego absentee miscount was caught only because paper ballots allowed a hand recount.

The closing section notes gains: California required voter-verifiable paper records by 2006, most recent presidential votes were cast on paper, and all 50 states now have post-election audit laws. Federal certification still does not require source code review, vendors still pay the test labs, and major manufacturers have not taken part in the village. The practical takeaway is that a record the voter can check matters more than a receipt.

talks.title: Colorado’s Creation of RLAs to Verify Election Results
talks.teaser: Traces how Colorado built statewide risk-limiting audits, from the 2009 law through the 2017 rollout, and why they verify vote tabulation.
talks.summary:
Wayne Williams, a former Colorado Secretary of State, explains how the state moved from unverified machine counts to statewide risk-limiting audits. He starts with the wider election process, arguing that every voting method has weaknesses, and says machine tabulation is more accurate than hand tallies but still needs independent checking. Older audits sampled a few precincts, so they could miss errors elsewhere in the state.

He then walks through the method. Sample size depends on how close a race is rather than on the total number of ballots, and each sampled paper ballot is compared against a machine-generated cast vote record, which the new voting systems had to produce. Colorado passed the law in 2009 but did not reach statewide use until 2017, after counties adopted compliant systems and an Election Assistance Commission pilot helped. Staff worked with small counties on new deadlines, used an open-source sampling tool built with an outside group, and drew random seeds from ten-sided dice rolled in public. The risk limit tightened from nine percent to three over time, and failed rounds lead to more sampling and eventually a full hand count.

His closing point is that an audit does not solve every election problem, such as ineligible voting or voter suppression, but it gives the public a verifiable basis for trust. He encourages other states to review their own post-election audits and adopt the parts of Colorado's approach that fit their systems.

talks.title: Beyond Casting and Tallying Security for the Rest of - Elections
talks.teaser: Presents a study of usability failures in election administration, based on interviews and a survey of election officials.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the 2020 Georgia election, where long lines were blamed partly on voting cards that only worked in one orientation. The speaker argues that research has focused on casting and tallying votes, while the administrative systems around them, such as poll books, voter registration databases, ballot scanners and night-of reporting, get little study. Usability problems in those systems could matter for election integrity, so the question is how common they are and how officials cope.

To find out, the team trained as poll watchers and took poll worker training, then ran about 14 semi-structured interviews and a survey that produced 45 usable responses. Recordings were deleted after analysis under institutional review board and federal protections, so no respondent can be identified. About 73% of officials reported preventable mistakes, and roughly one in five believed usability failures could change final counts. One example involved a poll book that blocked an eligible voter, where the manager cancelled instead of proceeding, leaving a vote with no matching check-in record. Officials also described hardware faults, rural connectivity gaps, undocumented procedures, and peer-shared documentation, along with harassment and exhaustion.

The speaker closes by arguing that usability failures should be handled like vulnerabilities and that non-voter-facing election technology needs independent study. Other recommendations include legal protection for election workers, blameless postmortems, and anonymous reporting of equipment malfunctions. The findings were preliminary, and the paper was not yet public, so the team asked election officials for feedback before release.

talks.title: Separating News from Noise
talks.teaser: Two election officials sort recent election news into real risks and noise, covering foreign interference, federal retreat, voter-roll checks, mail ballots and late rule changes.
talks.summary:
A Maricopa County deputy CIO and a veteran election-security consultant, formerly with the EAC, use this session to sort election news into what deserves attention and what is noise. The discussion covers four themes: foreign interference, changes in federal posture, claims of illegal voting, and late changes to rules.

On foreign interference, the consultant argues that recently published material largely repeated earlier federal assessments, and that the federal election-security staff has been depleted. He still expects adversaries to try to shape elections, with Iran singled out, and warns that victims once kept anonymous are now being named, which could expose officials to targeting. Reduced federal funding and pending DOJ lawsuits over voter rolls were described as drains on election offices' time. On citizenship checks, the speakers say snapshot results from the federal SAVE database produce false positives, and one state review found only 13 illegal votes over four years.

For late changes, the Purcell principle was raised as a reason to avoid altering rules close to an election. Late edits raise the chance of errors, which canvassing and certification are designed to catch. Proposed postal rules drew heavy public comment, and voters were advised to return ballots in person or at drop boxes. The takeaway is to check primary sources and ask whether a headline reflects a real change in risk.

talks.title: Evidence-Based Elections and Risk-Limiting Audits
talks.teaser: Explains risk-limiting audits, which use random ballot sampling to confirm that reported election winners really won, and why they depend on a trustworthy paper trail.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that counting an election by procedure is not enough. Election officials should be able to show affirmative evidence that the reported winners really won, and physical security, chain of custody, and rigorous ballot accounting are what make that possible. The speaker traces how audit thinking moved from checking whether machines work correctly, to detecting miscounts, to a standard built around correcting wrong outcomes.

The core method is the risk-limiting audit, defined by a known maximum chance of failing to correct a wrong result. The speaker explains ballot polling, where ballots are drawn at random and the audit keeps sampling until the evidence is strong enough, or until it falls back to a full hand count. A betting-game analogy and a 1939 inequality show why a large winning stake is unlikely if the reported outcome is false. The talk also covers how audits handle multiple contests and social choice rules, and gives workload figures for a large county.

The closing section warns about misuse. Audits run after certification, audits that check only a few contests, and audits built on an untrustworthy paper trail do not limit risk and can hide real problems. Practitioners should verify ballot accounting, chain of custody, and a trustworthy upper bound on ballots before auditing.

talks.title: Anomalies Are Not Normal
talks.teaser: Argues that election security failures persist when known vulnerabilities become normalized, drawing on the Challenger and Columbia investigations and a Georgia voting lawsuit.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with Curling v. Raffensperger, the Georgia lawsuit over Dominion ballot-marking devices. The plaintiffs presented many vulnerabilities that both sides' experts validated, yet the judge dismissed the case in 2025 because no one could demonstrate concrete harm. The speaker frames this as a failure of institutional decision-making rather than a failure of technical discovery.

To explain the gap, the talk recalls the Challenger investigation, where a demonstration with an O-ring in ice water made the cold-weather risk concrete, and the later Columbia loss, which the review traced to normalization of deviance: repeated anomalies accepted because schedules and operations took priority. The speaker maps foam strikes onto election flaws. A state-commissioned MITRE report labeled several issues as potential loss-of-vehicle events, but officials still treated the elections as successful and the issues as irrelevant.

The takeaway for researchers and program managers is to stop treating each bug as a standalone finding and to build a theory of risk that refuses to accept known deviations. The speaker argues that election security is a canary for other civic software, so the same pattern is likely to recur there.
